title: Levels of Cellular Organisation
subtitle: Unicellular, colonial and multicellular life
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: Compare the characteristics and structures of cells in unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms
lessonIntent: Students can compare the characteristics and structures of cells in unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms, and justify why a specialised cell cannot live independently.
examSkill: Compare the three levels on the same criteria (cell number, specialisation, independence, structures) and use interdependence, not cell count, to classify an organism.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, how life goes from one cell doing everything to whole organisms. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Why can a pond Amoeba live alone, but your liver cell can’t?
scenes.body: Organisation differs in cell specialisation, coordination and interdependence.
scenes.callout: Classify using organisation and life history, not an isolation death test.
scenes.caption: Unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisation form a continuum.

voiceover.text: An Amoeba is an entire organism in one cell. A liver cell belongs to a multicellular organism and depends on a controlled environment and support from other tissues. Some algae form groups of connected cells. These examples let us compare unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisation. But the boundary is a spectrum: Volvox carteri has specialised reproductive and somatic cells. And an isolated animal cell can survive in suitable culture, so cell death in pond water is not a classification test.

scenes.heading: One cell that does everything
scenes.body: A unicellular organism is a single cell that carries out every function of life on its own.

bullets.text: Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, yeast and bacteria.
One cell handles nutrition, respiration, excretion, movement, sensitivity and reproduction.
So the cell is a generalist, carrying extra structures: pseudopodia, a contractile vacuole.

scenes.callout: One cell, every job: a structural generalist.
scenes.caption: An Amoeba moves and feeds with pseudopodia and pumps out water with a contractile vacuole.

verdict.text: One generalist cell performs every function of life

voiceover.text: Start at the simplest level. A unicellular organism is an organism whose whole body is one single cell, like an Amoeba, a Paramecium, yeast or bacteria. That one cell has to do every job of staying alive, nutrition, respiration, getting rid of waste, moving, sensing its surroundings and reproducing. So it's a generalist, and it carries structures a specialised cell would never need. An Amoeba pushes out pseudopodia to move and to engulf its food. And a contractile vacuole fills with the water that leaks in from the pond, then pumps it back out. One cell, every job.

scenes.heading: Colonial life: together, but independent
scenes.body: Colonies vary in differentiation and integration; Volvox is not an identical-cell example.

bullets.text: Colonial groups vary in specialisation and integration.
Volvox carteri has reproductive and somatic cells.
Use coordination, cell roles and life history as evidence.

scenes.callout: The colonial–multicellular boundary is a continuum.
scenes.caption: Volvox illustrates differentiation within a colonial or simple multicellular alga.

voiceover.text: Colonial organisation means cells living together in an organised group. Some simple colonies have little cell differentiation; other groups show stronger integration. Volvox is often introduced as a colonial green alga, but Volvox carteri has specialised somatic cells and reproductive cells. It therefore illustrates the transition towards integrated multicellularity, rather than identical independent cells. Look at the evidence for specialisation, coordinated activity and reproduction, and state the convention you are using.

scenes.heading: Multicellular: specialised and dependent
scenes.body: Specialised cells and tissues cooperate in complex multicellular organisms.

bullets.text: Cell differentiation supports division of labour.
Separated cells may survive in suitable culture.

scenes.callout: Interdependence does not imply immediate death in isolation.
scenes.caption: Organisation and life history establish multicellularity.

voiceover.text: In a complex multicellular organism, specialised cells and tissues cooperate. Nerve cells transmit signals, red blood cells transport oxygen and gut cells absorb nutrients. Their division of labour supports the whole organism and creates interdependence. That does not mean every separated cell immediately dies: many animal cells can survive in a suitable culture medium. Classification depends on organised integration and the organism’s life cycle, not whether one cell survives an unsuitable isolation experiment.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Five terms for comparing the three levels.

bullets.text: Unicellular: one cell forms the organism.
Colonial: an organised cell group; integration and differentiation vary.
Multicellular: multiple coordinated cells form an organism.
Differentiation: features suited to particular functions.
Interdependence: reliance on other cells or tissues.

scenes.callout: State the evidence and classification convention.
scenes.caption: Classify cell groups using organisation, coordination and life history.

voiceover.text: Unicellular means one cell forms the organism and performs its life functions. Colonial means cells living in an organised group, with varying degrees of differentiation and integration. Multicellular means an organism comprises multiple coordinated cells; complex examples have specialised tissues. Cell specialisation, or differentiation, is development of features suited to particular functions. Interdependence is reliance on other cells or tissues for support in the organism. These categories are useful, but transitions are gradual and different conventions may classify simple algae differently.

scenes.heading: The liver cell and the Amoeba
scenes.question: Explain why pond water may support a freshwater Amoeba but damage a liver cell. Does this prove all multicellular cells must die in isolation?
scenes.coachNote: Explain environmental requirements; avoid treating unsuitable culture as a classification test.
steps: A freshwater Amoeba feeds independently and expels excess water with a contractile vacuole.
A liver cell normally receives nutrients and controlled conditions from surrounding tissues and blood.
Pond water is unsuitable culture medium and can cause osmotic swelling.
The comparison shows different requirements, not a universal isolation-death rule.
Animal cells can survive in suitable culture; classification uses organisation and life history.
scenes.caption: Adaptation to pond water differs from survival in suitable cell culture.

voiceover.text: Consider a hypothetical liver cell placed in pond water while a freshwater Amoeba thrives there. The Amoeba is adapted to freshwater: it feeds with pseudopodia and expels excess water using a contractile vacuole. The liver cell normally receives nutrients and controlled osmotic conditions through blood and surrounding tissue. Pond water does not provide suitable culture conditions, and its low solute concentration can damage the cell by osmotic swelling. This comparison shows different environmental requirements. It does not prove all multicellular cells must die alone: animal cells can survive in suitable culture.

scenes.heading: A colony is just a multicellular organism?
scenes.body: Wrong: identical independent cells always mean colonial; isolated-cell death always means multicellular.
scenes.secondary: Right: differentiation, integration and life history provide evidence, and the boundary is a continuum.
scenes.caption: Specialisation and integration vary among cell groups.

voiceover.text: A colony and a complex multicellular organism are not distinguished simply by the number of cells, or by whether separated cells die. Cell roles, coordination, integration and life history provide better evidence. Some colonies have specialised cell types, and isolated cells from a multicellular organism may survive in suitable culture. Volvox carteri is a useful boundary example because reproductive and somatic cells have different roles.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: X is a single Amoeba; Y is a coordinated algal group with little differentiation; Z has specialised tissues and organs. Describe their organisation.
answerSteps: Y: colonial organisation under the convention used here.
Use differentiation, coordination and life history; isolation survival is not decisive.
scenes.caption: Organisation and life history support classification.

voiceover.text: Quick check. X is one Amoeba cell that feeds and reproduces as an organism. Y is a coordinated group of algal cells with little differentiation. Z has specialised tissues and organs. How would you describe them? Pause. X is unicellular. Y shows colonial organisation under the convention used here. Z is a complex multicellular organism. These descriptions use organisation and life history. They do not establish whether every isolated cell can survive, and more integrated algal groups can sit near the boundary.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Unicellular: one cell forms the organism.
Colonial groups vary in differentiation and integration.
Complex multicellular organisms coordinate specialised cells and tissues.
Volvox carteri has differentiated reproductive and somatic cells.
Isolated-cell survival is not a decisive classification test.
scenes.finalPrompt: Compare cell roles, integration and life history.
scenes.caption: Organisation is a continuum; classification requires evidence.

voiceover.text: Unicellular organisms consist of one cell. Colonial groups vary in differentiation and integration. Complex multicellular organisms have coordinated specialised cells, often organised into tissues and organs. Volvox carteri has reproductive and somatic differentiation, so the boundary is not a simple identical-cell rule. Isolated animal cells may survive in suitable culture. Compare organisation, cell roles and life history, and explain the convention you use.
